chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
The 'Aqilah (blood relatives) are not liable/guarantors for deliberate (killing), nor for confession, nor for reconciliation.

key_terms.إِقْرَاراً: Confession; referring to the legal act of confessing to a crime.
key_terms.الْعَاقِلَةُ: The 'Aqilah: the group of male relatives responsible for paying blood money (diyah) in Islamic law.
key_terms.صُلْحاً: Reconciliation; referring to a settlement agreement regarding blood money or compensation.
key_terms.عَمْداً: Deliberately/intentionally; referring to deliberate homicide where the 'Aqilah's liability may differ.

ai.seo_question: What are the exceptions to the 'Aqilah's liability for blood money in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delineates the financial liability of the 'Aqilah, clarifying that their guarantee covers only accidental homicide and excludes deliberate killing, personal confession, or private settlement agreements. This distinction is crucial in Shia jurisprudence for determining when the extended kinship group assumes responsibility versus when it remains with the individual, reflecting the principle of 'Aqilah as a social safety net rather than a blanket insurer.
